short: In 28 BCE Augustus conducted the first empire-wide census, establishing the assessment system that underpinned Roman taxation for centuries.
full:
In 28 BCE, Augustus carried out a census of Roman citizens, the first in forty-one years, recording just over four million names, and, more significantly for the provinces, began the long process of assessing the whole empire for taxation, something no earlier Roman government had attempted systematically. He repeated the exercise in 8 BCE and again in 14 CE, according to his own account in the Res Gestae.

Provincial assessments proceeded unevenly, region by region, over years rather than all at once, recording land, population and property to calculate the land tax and the poll tax. The resulting registers gave Rome, for the first time, a reasonably systematic picture of its empire's resources, and the census-based assessment they established remained the basis of Roman taxation until Diocletian overhauled it at the end of the third century.
